title: Webex APIs, bots, and xAPI
blurb: Bots, integrations, messaging webhooks, and cloud xAPI commands against devices you are allowed to touch.

lessons.title: Bots and integrations
lessons.summary: A bot is a member of a space. An integration acts as a user who granted OAuth. A personal access token is neither of those in production.
objectives: Keep personal tokens out of production
Cite the getting started page for token lifetime

diagram.caption: Pick the actor before you pick the URL.

steps.label: Create a bot when the actor is the bot
steps.detail: The bot has a name, a username, and a token. People add it to spaces.

steps.label: Use OAuth when the actor is a person
steps.detail: The integration requests scopes. The token represents that user.

steps.label: Read the personal token rules
steps.detail: The Webex developer getting started page describes personal access tokens for trying the API, including a 12-hour expiry. That page is not the contact center guide.

steps.label: Call with the right token
steps.detail: A bot token sees bot-scoped data. A user token sees what that user may see.

sections.h: Twelve hours, from the general guide
paragraphs: Personal access tokens expire 12 hours after they are issued, on the getting started page this lab uses. Confirm the live sentence before you quote it in a runbook, and do not put one in a server.
Contact center production access uses the contact center scopes and integration model, not this shortcut.
A bot is not an agent desktop profile and not a virtual agent. Those are contact center objects.
A bot is not an xAPI command. xAPI is how an authorized app talks to a device.

cards.back: OAuth on behalf of a user.

lessons.summary: In a group space a bot receives messages that mention it. In a one-to-one space it receives the messages in that conversation.

paragraphs: If you need every message in a large space, a bot is the wrong tool. The guide does not give the bot a hidden transcript of the room.

lessons.title: Messaging webhooks
lessons.summary: Create a webhook with a secret. Verify X-Spark-Signature as HMAC-SHA1, and prefer X-Webex-Signature when the newer header is present. A listener that fails too often is disabled.
objectives: Verify the signature over raw bytes

steps.label: Create the webhook with a secret
steps.detail: The target URL must be reachable by Webex. The secret is what you verify with.

steps.label: POST the notification
steps.detail: Respond in the 2xx range. The guide disables a webhook after 100 failed attempts within five minutes.

steps.label: Check X-Spark-Signature
steps.detail: HMAC-SHA1 over the unmodified raw body. Header names are case-insensitive. HTTP/2 may deliver the header in lowercase.

steps.label: Prefer X-Webex-Signature when it is present
steps.detail: The guide says that header carries HMAC-SHA256 and HMAC-SHA512 for supported types. Use the algorithm the header indicates.

paragraphs: Compute the HMAC before parsing or re-serializing JSON. A pretty printer changes the bytes and the signature fails.
The messaging guide says this explicitly, and it says HMAC-SHA1 is documented because it is the header contract, not as general cryptographic advice.

sections.h: Contact center is the other header
paragraphs: X-WebexCC-Signature is HMAC-SHA256 for contact center subscriptions. Do not reuse this messaging function unchanged.
The disable rule in this lesson is the messaging rule: 100 failures in five minutes.

quiz.why: When the webhook was created with a secret.

choices: Carries SHA256 and SHA512 for supported types
In constant time, before you trust the payload
With a normal string equals after parsing

lab.title: Failure budget
lab.goal: Write how your listener stays under the disable threshold.

steps.expect: You reject without looping retries at Webex

fault.title: Pretty-printed HMAC
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: HMAC computed after JSON.stringify of a parsed object.

steps.detail: No reply on a bad signature.

steps.detail: The bots guide shows how a bot posts a message. Start there.

steps.detail: Interactive cards exist in Webex messaging. This lab will not embed a sample payload, because copying a stale schema is how bots ship broken UI.

steps.label: Redact

sections.h: Why there is no sample card
paragraphs: A card payload is an API schema. The honest way to teach it is to point at the developer page that currently publishes the example.
If you need a card, copy it from that page on the day you build, and cite the URL in your commit.
Mention in, text out, signature checked, 2xx returned. That loop is the whole lesson.
Contact center screen pop is not a messaging card.

lessons.title: Cloud xAPI commands
lessons.summary: An authorized integration can POST a command to a device in the same organization. The URL is the Webex xAPI command resource. The device must be granted.
objectives: Stay inside the organization and the grant
Read RoomOS xAPI for the command name

diagram.caption: Same org. Granted device. One command.

flow.title: Ask a room device for its status

steps.label: Find the command on RoomOS xAPI
steps.detail: roomos.cisco.com/xapi is the command catalog. Do not invent a command name.
steps.inspect: Device developer guide for the cloud path

steps.label: POST /v1/xapi/command/{commandName}
steps.detail: The execute-command guide documents that URL on https://webexapis.com.

steps.label: The device must be in your org and granted to the app
steps.detail: The device developer guide limits bots and integrations to devices they are allowed to control.
steps.inspect: A MAC you can see is not permission

steps.label: Read the result
steps.detail: Errors include auth, missing grant, and a device that is offline. The status commands are a different resource from commands.

paragraphs: The execute-command page is for commands. Status is a different xAPI surface. Mixing them produces a 404 that looks like an outage.
Macros that run on the device itself are yet another path, covered with devices.
A bot can be used where the device guide allows it, still only in the same organization and only on granted devices.
A bot that can talk in a space cannot automatically pan a camera.

choices: In the same organization and granted

quiz.why: A 404 may mean the wrong one.

choices: Does not automatically gain device control
quiz.why: Grant it, if the guide allows that app type.

choices: Are a separate path from cloud xAPI

fault.title: Wrong org
fault.symptom: The command returns an authorization error for a device you can see in a screenshot.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: device belongs to another organization.

fault.fix: Use a device in the token's organization that the integration is allowed to control.

lessons.title: Scopes and grants
lessons.summary: OAuth scopes are the menu. Device grants are the specific rooms. Asking for every scope is how tokens become dangerous.
objectives: Request only the scopes the call needs
Separate this from contact center scopes

diagram.caption: Least scope, then an explicit device.

steps.label: Read the scope list
steps.detail: The device developer guide names the scopes for cloud xAPI. Copy from there.

steps.label: Grant the room
steps.detail: Same organization. The grant is the allow-list.
steps.inspect: Remove it when the pilot ends

steps.label: Send one command
steps.detail: Log the command name and the device id, not the token.

steps.label: Remove unused integrations
steps.detail: A token that can post messages and move cameras is two jobs. Split them if the portal lets you.

sections.h: Contact center scopes are a different list
paragraphs: cjp:config and cjp:config_read belong to the contact center search reference. They do not grant xAPI.
A single integration can request several families only if you mean to. Prefer two apps.

sections.h: Workspace admin is not this token
paragraphs: Control Hub device admin and an API token are different doors. Being a full administrator does not paste a scope onto a bot.
Cross-launch of Dedicated Instance is a third door.

choices: Which device the app may control
Command name and device id, not the token
Is not an API scope by itself
Two apps, when you can split them
A macro with the token inside

fault.title: Token in a macro
fault.symptom: A room device contains a cloud token in a macro that was emailed around.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: macro source includes a bearer token.
fault.cause: The device does not need your cloud token to run a local macro, and the token is now copied.
fault.fix: Revoke the token and load a macro with no secret.

lessons.title: A small, safe bot loop
lessons.summary: Mention, verify, reply with text, and stop. Device commands stay in a different app. Nothing in this lab calls the live API.

diagram.caption: The loop fits on a card.

flow.title: The only loop this lesson wants

steps.label: Deliver the event
steps.detail: Group events are mentions. 1:1 events are the conversation.

steps.label: Verify before parsing
steps.detail: X-Spark-Signature or X-Webex-Signature as the guide prefers.

steps.label: Post text as the bot
steps.detail: No card until you have copied a current example. No secrets in the text.

steps.label: Return 2xx promptly
steps.detail: 100 failures in five minutes disables the webhook.

paragraphs: Camera controls are a second integration with device scopes and grants.
A webhook handler that also sends xAPI is how a mention moves a camera. Split the processes.

fault.title: Retry storm
fault.symptom: The listener crashes, Webex retries, and the webhook disables itself.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: 100 HTTP 500 responses in four minutes.
fault.fix: Return 2xx only after you have safely stored a valid event, and alert before the hundredth failure.
